source.title: BioVFM-21M: Benchmarking and Scaling Self-Supervised Vision Foundation Models for Biomedical Image Analysis
source.authors: Jia-Run Liu; Hong-Yu Zhou; Weijian Huang; Hao Yang; Dongning Song; Tao Tan; Yong Liang; Shan Wang

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present. Some figure data are not recoverable from the flattened text.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling behavior in biomedical vision models using downstream AUC and fitted performance curves, rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study reports scaling results for model size, data size, and modality, plus differences across tasks and pretraining algorithms. It does not report held-out loss, language-model runs, compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, or fixed-parameter architecture comparisons. Values cited only from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Scales self-supervised biomedical vision encoders (5–303M params; data and modality subsets) and fits power functions to linear-probe AUC on 12 MedMNIST tasks. This is a new setting (medical vision, downstream metric) with its own results on whether performance scales with size. It is T3 rather than T2 because it measures downstream AUC, not held-out loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find scaling helps medical vision foundation models, but benefits vary with task complexity, data diversity (more than data size) and the pretraining algorithm. They say simpler tasks may not justify the cost of scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Biomedical self-supervised vision-model size and data/modality sweeps; evaluates downstream MedMNIST AUC and fits performance scaling curves, rather than measuring held-out language-model cross-entropy or compute-optimal language-model allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported scaling slopes and gains vary across pretraining algorithms, evaluation benchmarks, and data settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-task scaling slopes correlate with benchmark properties (sample count, DBI positive; gzip compressibility negative). The relative ranking of task slopes is stable across pretraining methods.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The size of downstream scaling benefit is predictable from task data properties.

record.problems: The scaling outcomes are downstream AUC, not held-out pretraining loss. Scaling uncertainty and goodness-of-fit statistics are not reported in the text. Several task-specific curve values appear only in figures, and the text does not always identify which pretraining algorithm an example concerns.
record.rows_left_out: Task-specific fitted slope values displayed in Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 are not individually recorded because the flattened text does not reliably associate all plotted values with benchmarks and algorithms.

untested.parts: No language models and no held-out pretraining loss.
No extrapolation from small to much larger runs.
Loss-based power law in vision, video, repeated data and fine-tuning/transfer scaling are not tested; only downstream AUC vs model size is fitted.
Prediction of downstream performance from pretraining loss, and extrapolation accuracy, are not tested.
Parameter counting, schedules, fitting-method sensitivity and compute-optimal split disagreements are not tested; only slope dependence on SSL algorithm and task is shown.

missing.what: Per-task, per-algorithm fitted slopes (e.g. pairs like D 0.0224/M 0.0452, D 0.0141/M 0.0692) and their benchmark association
Stable cross-method ordering of task slopes; high/low-slope group gap of 3–14 fold
Pearson correlations of slopes with sample count, DBI and gzip compressibility (no numbers in the text)

record.verdict_notes: The outcome is linear-probe AUC, not loss. AUC is bounded near ceiling on many MedMNIST tasks, which may compress slopes. Only one setup per size, with no CIs on the scaling points and no fit statistics. Rows r8, r10 and r11 concern diversity, not scale. The BioVFM 630M vs other models comparison (Table 1) is the authors' own model against others and is correctly not recorded as a row.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss and power-law behavior in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations as compute changes.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests biomedical image models and downstream AUC, not held-out loss; does not test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Tests downstream benchmark AUC across model scales, not downstream performance predicted from pretraining loss.
Reports variation by task and pretraining algorithm, but does not test parameter-counting choices, training schedules, fitting-method sensitivity, or compute-optimal splits.

relationships.condition: Biomedical ViT encoders, model size 5–303M, mean linear-probe AUC (DINOv2 and MAE)
relationships.reason: Both algorithms improve mean AUC with size (2.1%, 2.3%) and a power function is fitted (slopes 0.0088, 0.0191); r1–r4. Fit quality is not reported.
relationships.display_finding: DINOv2 and MAE improved mean AUC by 2.1% and 2.3%, respectively, with fitted power-function slopes of 0.0088 and 0.0191 and no reported fit quality.

relationships.reason: Slopes vary over 40-fold across tasks, RetinaMNIST plateaus past 21.7M, and 100x data gives only +0.2% AUC; r5, r7, r9.
relationships.display_finding: Slopes varied over 40-fold across tasks, RetinaMNIST plateaued beyond 21.7M, and 100-fold more data yielded only +0.2% AUC.

relationships.condition: Mean downstream AUC and ChestMNIST as model size grows
relationships.reason: Downstream AUC rises with model size for both algorithms and on ChestMNIST by 4.65%; r1, r2, r6.
relationships.display_finding: Downstream AUC rises with model size for both algorithms, including a 4.65% increase on ChestMNIST.

relationships.reason: Gains are strongly task-dependent and plateau on some tasks; data scaling gives diminishing returns; r5, r7, r9.
relationships.display_finding: Gains differed substantially across tasks, plateaued on some tasks and diminished as training data increased.

relationships.condition: Different SSL pretraining objectives and evaluation tasks
relationships.reason: Fitted slopes differ about 2x between MAE and DINOv2 and over 40-fold across tasks; r3, r4, r5.
relationships.display_finding: Fitted slopes differ by about twofold between MAE and DINOv2 and by over 40-fold across evaluation tasks.
